surfaces.part: top cap band of the pillar
ice shaft (main body, vertical faceted face)

answer.evidence: The main body is a tall shaft (rows 7-39) with blue shading on the right and horizontal dark crack lines, all drawn as a vertical face. The top cap (rows 3-6) is a flat band: row 3 is outline, rows 4-5 are white, row 6 is a lighter edge line, and rows 7-9 are a slightly darker shadow. Its width is 9 on all four rows, so it has no ellipse profile; it never narrows above, and it is a flat-band cap like the 'column: flat band cap' wrong reference. The bottom rows 40-46 widen and narrow again (11, 14, 16, 16, 14, 12) as a snowy base mound, but that is a pedestal, not the main body's top surface. The shaft shows no top surface beyond the thin cap band, so it reads as a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin, small ice pillar with a capital and base, about one tile wide and two tiles tall. The reference trees are far larger leafy canopies, so I judged the candidate by eye as a sparse object. Measured facts: 15 visible tones per tile, above tree-1a786c (7) and below tree-d43edd (29). Near-flat coverage is 0%, so there are no large flat fills. Dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outline is tinted: a darker blue-teal tone of the ice, not black. By eye, the shaft has about 5 lightness steps (white highlight, pale blue, mid blue, shadow blue, dark blue edge) with fluting and facet variation. It reads as shaded form and not a flat body with an outline. The capital and base have some chipped, grainy detail. It is less textured than the big canopy reference but is not thinner or more sticker-like than the simpler reference, so a careful artist would accept it beside the references.

answer.evidence: The pillar is a tall shaft with light and dark vertical shading (rows 7-39). Its top is a flat band, rows 3-6, 9 px wide on a 7-8 px shaft. The width is constant at 9 over rows 3-6 and drops straight to 8 at row 7, so it never widens and then narrows. That makes it a flat-bottomed cap, not an ellipse. Row 3 is outline, rows 4-5 are white and row 6 is a thin lighter edge line. Rows 7-9 hold only a little darker blue at the right side, not a clear eave shadow, so the top reads as a 2-row rim. The wider base (rows 40-46, widths 14-16-12) is a puddle or mound at the bottom and is not the pillar's top. No side face is drawn. This matches the reference 'column: flat band cap' (wrong) rather than the ellipse cap (right).

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin, sparse object (a broken ice column), so I judged density by eye as well as by the numbers. The facts support it: 15 visible tones per tile is above tree-1a786c (7) and below tree-d43edd (29), near-flat coverage is 0%, and 0% of the dark edge pixels are neutral. That means the outline is a dark blue-tinted version of the ice, not a black sticker line. The column shows about 5 lightness steps: white highlight, pale ice, mid blue, shadow blue, and deep blue. It also has fluting lines and a chipped top and base. It carries less texture than the rich tree canopies, but no large areas are flat fills. A careful artist would accept it next to the references as an equally crafted prop that is simply smaller and simpler.

answer.evidence: The main body is a tall tapering ice shaft in rows 7-39, drawn as a vertical face with light-to-dark vertical shading and no horizontal surface. The top cap in rows 3-6 is a flat band of constant width 9. Its top row is already full width, so it never narrows above, which means it is a flat cap rather than an ellipse. Only about 2 white rows (4-5) could pass as a top, followed by an edge row at 6 and a slight narrowing to width 8, so it reads as a rim, like the 'column: flat band cap' reference. The flared base in rows 40-46 widens from 14 to 16 and narrows to 12 and is a mound at the foot, not a top surface of the shaft. Overall this is a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin, upright ice column with a capital and a base. It is a sparse object, so I judged density by eye. The measured facts support it: 15 visible tones per tile sits between tree-1a786c (7) and tree-d43edd (29), near-flat coverage is 0%, and 0% of the dark edge pixels are neutral. The outline is a dark blue-teal that leans toward the adjacent ice rather than a neutral black line, and some edges are separated by value alone. The column shows about 5 lightness steps: bright highlight, pale ice, mid blue, shadow blue and a deep edge. It also has facet and crack variation and a lit left edge with a shaded right side. This reads as a rounded form, not a flat sticker. It is simpler than the rich canopy of tree-d43edd, but it is as rich as the weaker reference tree-1a786c and has no large flat fills. A careful artist would accept it next to the references, though the kind match is loose because the candidate is a pillar rather than foliage.

answer.evidence: The main body is the shaft, rows 7-39, drawn as a vertical face with a light-to-dark side gradient. Its top cap, rows 3-6, has a constant width of 9 in the silhouette profile. The flared base, rows 40-46, widens from 14 to 16 and narrows again to 12, so it has an ellipse-like footing. It is a small plinth rather than the main body. The pillar's own top therefore shows no real top surface.
